title: Someone keeps telling you your memory is wrong
lede: You remember the conversation. They say it never happened, or happened completely differently, and they say it with total confidence and a note of concern for you. It has happened enough times that you have started checking yourself before you speak.

blocks.text: You remember the conversation. They say it never happened, or happened completely differently, and they say it with total confidence and a note of concern for you. It has happened enough times that you have started checking yourself before you speak.

items: The tell is not the disagreement. Two people remember things differently all the time. The tell is the pattern: it is always your memory that is faulty, and their certainty always arrives with pity attached.
The goal of this behaviour is not to win an argument about Tuesday. It is to make your own judgement feel unreliable, so that theirs becomes the only usable instrument in the room.
The exhaustion is the point. Once you are tired enough, agreeing is cheaper than remembering, and that is the state being engineered.
You are probably already doing the thing people in this position do: apologising pre-emptively and rehearsing sentences before you say them.

items.move: Start writing things down, privately, the same day
items.detail: Date, what was said, exact phrases. Not to build a case — to give yourself an external memory that cannot be edited by conversation.

items.move: Stop arguing about the facts of the past
items.detail: You will not win it and every round trains you to doubt yourself further. Argue nothing; record everything.
Move agreements to text and email. "Just confirming what we said" is the single most protective habit available to you.

items.move: Say the disagreement once, calmly, and hold it
items.detail: You do not need them to concede. You need to practise not folding, which is a separate skill from being right.
Isolation is what makes this work. One person who knows the full pattern breaks its power substantially.

items.move: Watch what happens when you hold your ground
items.detail: Reasonable people get uncomfortable. People running a play escalate — anger, tears, threats, or sudden warmth. The escalation is diagnostic.

items.say: "I remember it differently, and I am not going to argue about it. I know what I heard."
"Let us put it in a message so neither of us has to rely on memory."
"This is the fourth time I have been told my memory is wrong. I have started writing things down."
"I am not confused and I am not unwell. I disagree with you."

items: Demanding they admit it. Admission is the one thing this behaviour is structured to never give.
Presenting your notes as evidence in an argument. It converts your safety net into ammunition and it will be attacked.
Accepting "you are being paranoid" as a data point about you. It is a data point about them.
Deciding on your future during a bad night. Decide in daylight, with the notes in front of you.
Read your notes weekly. Patterns are invisible day to day and obvious across a month.
Rebuild one outside relationship you have let slide. Isolation is the load-bearing wall of this dynamic.
Notice how you feel physically after contact with them. The body registers this earlier than the mind and it is worth listening to.
If this is a partner or family member, consider a therapist who is briefed on coercive control specifically, not general couples work.

limit: If this comes with control of your money, your phone, your movements, or your contact with others, or with threats and intimidation, it is coercive control — a recognised and in many places criminal pattern of abuse. Contact a domestic abuse service, which can advise confidentially and safely.
